title: Hedge laying basics
subtitle: Restoring a gappy or overgrown hedge to a stockproof boundary.
excerpt: Hedge laying is the traditional British technique for rejuvenating a hedge that has grown too tall, gone leggy at the base, or developed gaps that livestock can push through. The stems are partially cut and laid at an angle, encouraging vigorous new growth from the base and creating a thick, stockproof barrier. A skilled layer works at roughly 20 metres per day.
sourceNotes: National Hedgelaying Society, An Introduction to Hedgelaying (2019). Jake Fiennes, Land: How the Hunger for Ownership Shaped the Modern World (2022), hedges chapter. John Wright, Hedgerow (2010).

glossaryTerms.definition: A stem that has been cut almost through near the base and laid at an angle of 30 to 45 degrees to the ground. The sap continues to flow through the uncut wood, keeping the stem alive.
A flexible shoot (hazel or willow) woven along the top of the laid hedge between the vertical stakes to hold everything in place and add height.

content.text: Hedge laying is done in late autumn to early spring when the sap is down. Working in the growing season risks the tree failing to heal the cut. Hawthorn, blackthorn, hazel, ash, and field maple all lay well. Pure single-species hawthorn hedges are the most common subject on working smallholdings.
Clear all dead material, brambles, and woody debris from the base of the hedge. This exposes the main stems and gives you clear access for the laying cuts.
Remove any stems that are dead, diseased, or too thick to lay (over 12 to 15 cm diameter at the base). Stems this size are left as standard trees or cut out entirely. They cannot be laid cleanly.

is the critical skill. Use a billhook to cut a diagonal slice from the front face of the stem starting 15 to 20 cm above ground level. Work the cut downward and toward the direction of lay, removing wood but leaving a hinge of bark and sapwood on the back of the stem. The hinge must remain unbroken: if it splits, the stem cannot draw water and will die.
A well-placed cut leaves the stem at 30 to 45 degrees, leaning uphill or into the prevailing wind.
Work along the hedge in one direction, laying each stem over the previous one. The overlapping stems support each other.
Drive vertical stakes (hazel or ash, 60 to 90 cm above the finished height) at 50 to 60 cm intervals through the laid material.

Trim any upright shoots above the binder line for a tidy finish. This improves the look but also reduces the chance of deer catching on upright spurs.

attrs.cue: Pleacher is cracking across the hinge as you lay it
attrs.cause: Cutting too deep or at too sharp an angle; the hinge is too thin to support the weight of the stem
attrs.fix: Stop laying and re-cut higher up the stem. Use a shallower cut next time, leaving more wood at the back. A cracked hinge that still has a strip of bark intact may survive if you pack moss around it and secure with hessian.

attrs.cue: New growth is not shooting from the base after the first spring
attrs.cause: Cut was made when sap was already rising, or the soil at the base was very compacted
attrs.fix: New growth can be slow in the first season. If there is no growth by midsummer, the stem has likely failed to draw water. Remove it and treat the gap with a transplanted whip or tube-planted bare root species.
